Learning Objectives
Review barriers to effective patient communication and determine how personal background
may affect the manner in which a physician is perceived.
Assess how shared decision making, decision aids, and translators can positively affect a
patient’s experience and outcomes.
Address the general and unique differences within and between racial or ethnic patient
populations.
Appreciate the current initiatives promoting sex and racial diversity in the field of orthopaedic
surgery.
Cultural Competence and Communication

Communication skills are increasingly important for achieving successful outcomes with
orthopaedic patients, especially if orthopaedic surgeons are seen as high-tech, low-touch
physicians.
The patient population served by orthopaedic surgeons is becoming increasingly more diverse;
however, this is not yet reflected in the workforce.

Background
Projections based on the 2000 US census predict that minorities will make up more than
one-half of the US population by 2070.1 Physicians must improve their communication
skills to meet the diverse needs of this new and growing population. Communication
should be conceptualized as a source emitting information and a receiver taking in the
information and broadcasting feedback. Patients care about their surgeon’s level of
medical training and achieving successful medical results almost, if not just as much, as
their ability to listen, care, and show compassion; however, when polled, most surgeons
simply believe that results are most important to the patient.2 This observation is
complicated by a trend showing that a physician’s self-perceived effectiveness in
listening ability is scored substantially higher than the scores given by their patients.3
Simply, physicians have an inflated sense of ability to be empathetic and communicate,
and their patients are not receiving the communication they require. This does not bode
well for the future treatment of culturally diverse patient populations with which
communication already is difficult.
Barriers to Patient Communication
Language, literacy, and cultural differences are the three main barriers in the physician-patient
relationship. Often, the three barriers substantially coexist.
Effectively communicating and providing safe, high-quality, patient-centered care necessitate
overcoming these three barriers.
Language

9/3/26, 7:48 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
2/25

Referring to communication with a patient who reads, writes, or speaks in a language other
than English
Linguistic minorities receive poorer care than racial or ethnic minorities.

Language
Currently, 20 million people living in the United States have limited English-language
proficiency. In Portland, Oregon, alone, 210 different languages are spoken.2 Linguistic
minorities receive poorer care and have poorer outcomes than racial or ethnic
minorities.4 The barrier of language differences can be overcome through interpreter
services or by learning a language; however, learning a language is not the same as
understanding a culture, and interventions are necessary to enhance cultural
competence after language acquisition. In addition, patients may still be at risk for not
understanding because of limited health literacy.3
Literacy
Referring to the capacity to obtain, process, and understand basic health information and
services necessary to make appropriate health decisions despite effectively managing other
life aspects
The quality of health care is undermined if the patient does not understand his or her
treatment.

Literacy
Limited healthcare literacy affects 50% of adults but more ethnic minorities.5 Predictors
of low literacy may include low reading ability, low education level, advanced age,
Spanish-speaking, nonwhite race or ethnicity, or low income.3,6 Lower-literacy patients
ask fewer questions, are less involved in decision making regarding their health, and are
at greater risk for suboptimal outcomes and misuse of resources.3 Physicians treating
these patients may feel less connected, comfortable, or empathetic; take less patient-
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
3/25

centered approaches; and are more verbally dominant.3 Communication and decision
aids are critical in the education of patients to ensure greater understanding.
Cultural Differences
Referring to differences in beliefs, values, and thoughts that interfere with accurate
information exchange
Culture is “any group of people who share experiences, language, and values that permit them
to communicate knowledge not shared by those outside the culture.”2
African American, Hispanic, and Native American populations have 50% to 100% higher rates
of illness and mortality from chronic illnesses than Caucasian individuals even if insurance
status, income, age, education level, comorbidities, and severity of conditions are comparable.
Patient-focused care requires cross-cultural communication that is open and honest and
builds trust.

Cultural Differences
Culture includes language; thoughts; beliefs; values; actions; communication; and
institutions of racial, ethnic, religious, or social groups. These components are mutable,
may be multiple, and require context.7 Cross-cultural communication strains the doctor-
patient relationship. The patient and the physician project and broadcast their own
beliefs, values, and cultures, possibly concluding in miscommunication and, ultimately,
disparity in care.5 Physicians should develop skills for cross-cultural communication and
learn to explore the patient’s views of pain, sickness, and treatment.5 Whaley and Davis8
suggested that patients must “understand and accept their diagnosis as well as believe
that the recommended treatment programs offer them hope for satisfactory recovery.”
A patient is far less likely to understand or act on medical advice if their culture is not
considered.
Gardenswartz and Rowe9 described six realities of cultural programming that physicians
should consider to improve communication with patients from different cultures to
reduce healthcare disparities.2,5
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
4/25

Culture is not obvious.
Each individual believes that his or her culture is the best.
Individuals misinterpret the actions of others if their misinterpretations of their own
observations are not understood.
Individuals may not know if they are offending others.
Awareness of differences and possible barriers improves the likelihood of successful
interaction.
Understanding one’s own software or value system is a crucial step in providing
culturally competent care.
Ethnic and racial minorities experience poorer outcomes in orthopaedics.10 The causes
of healthcare disparity are numerous, complex, and evolving. Many point to institutional
racism, defined as the differential access to the goods, services, and opportunities of
society according to race and independent of all other factors.5 Therefore, the number
of knee arthroplasty procedures is substantially lower in minority populations, a trend
that persists even after controlling for income.11
Many also look to internalized racism, (ie, developed behaviors and attitudes about a
patient’s health care that are based on mistrust, resignation, helplessness, and
hopelessness, which may be based in real or perceived mistreatment, and that harm
interactions with the healthcare system).4 Separate from the biomedical treatment
received, minority patients report poorer physician-patient interactions.10
Before the advent of communication training, orthopaedic surgeons were known as
poor communicators by patients and colleagues, being more interested in finding and
fixing biomedical problems.2 Acknowledgement of a patient’s emotions, education,
occupation, economics, spiritual values, lifestyle, and family background is important in
determining an empathetic approach.2 Acknowledgement demonstrates empathy and
promotes more effective communication between the physician and patient, building
mutual trust and facilitating medical decision making. Misunderstandings resulting from
poor cross-cultural communication typically involve six topics: authority, physical
contact, communication styles, sex, sexuality, and family.2 Without open dialogue, the
likelihood of misunderstanding increases. Orthopaedic surgeons and their care teams
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
5/25

must prioritize efforts to develop and use nontechnical skills aimed at improving
interpersonal communication, ultimately improving patient satisfaction, communication,
and empathy.
Cultural Competence
The four major components of cultural competence are awareness, attitude, knowledge, and
skills.
Patients from varying cultures have different perceptions regarding health and illness and,
therefore, may have different beliefs regarding treatment and outcomes.
Achieving cultural competence is crucial for improving communication, patient satisfaction,
compliance, and outcomes.
Cultural competency education is crucial in meeting the needs of current and future patient
populations.

Cultural Competence
Cultural competence is the ability of providers to deliver health care that recognizes the
social, cultural, and linguistic needs of patients: race, ethnicity, sex, and faith.1,2,6,7,10
Pedersen’s conceptual framework for developing cultural and cross-cultural competence
identifies four components: awareness, attitude, knowledge, and skills.6 Awareness is
the fact that different cultures have different values. Attitude refers to the feeling an
individual has toward his or her own beliefs, which may collide with others if different.
Knowledge allows us to understand and avoid judging other cultures. Skills refer to the
crucial abilities allowing a physician to interact with a patient by putting his or her
competencies to use.
Many decisions made in musculoskeletal care are particularly sensitive to patient
preferences,3 which are primarily filtered through a patient’s culture, beliefs, and values.
This is why the concept of cultural competency is inextricably connected with patient-
centered care. Patient-centered care is a humanistic, evidence-based approach that
relies on empathy and effective communication skills to improve the quality of care and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
6/25

the patient experience while optimizing resource use.3 Therefore, a patient’s culture will
guide his or her perceptions of health, illness, and medical care. Cultural competence
allows the physician to communicate and connect with a patient on a deeper level. This
bond, via enhanced communication, is pivotal in facilitating shared decision making that
aligns with a patient’s belief system.
Illness, or the state of being unwell, consists of objective pathophysiologic disease and
subjective experience.3 Therefore patient satisfaction regarding treatment relies on
subjective experience, considering culture, beliefs, values, and attitudes, as well as
biomedical outcomes.5 Physicians seeking to drastically improve patient satisfaction
should use patient-centered evidence-based care applying cultural competency. A study
conducted in a hand surgery office demonstrated that 65% of the variation in patient
satisfaction was attributed to patient age, emotional health, patient activation, degree of
involvement in decision making, and expectations of care.3 By tailoring communication
to a patient’s cultural needs, physicians can improve patient satisfaction, perceived
quality of interaction, compliance, health outcomes, and informed medical decisions
while reducing rates of malpractice filing.5,6,10 Allowing patients to explain their story in
their own way; being sensitive to perceived discrimination; recognizing preferences for
face-to-face or electronic communication; and avoiding stereotypes, terms, and gestures
with perceived negative connotation may help establish a starting point for culturally
competent communication.
Recently, medicine has become more consumer focused, as exemplified by the rise in
pay-for-performance reimbursement popularity. The subjective experiential side of
health care, especially in regard to patient-reported outcomes and satisfaction, have
become increasingly important in this movement. Assessment of these factors will be
tied to physician reimbursement or financial incentives in the pay-for-performance
model. Currently, surveys such as the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers
and Systems (CAHPS) and the Press Ganey survey are being used to assess patient
satisfaction with their care; 30% of Medicaid reimbursement is tied to scores from these
surveys.3,10 The CAHPS is officially offered in English, Spanish, Chinese, Russian,
Vietnamese, Portuguese, and German translations. For other languages, the Agency for
Healthcare Research and Quality provides guidelines for effective and accurate
translation of the CAHPS, which may be extrapolated to other questionnaires. Simply
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
7/25

speaking another language is not adequate to appreciate cultural context. This trend
also is seen in patient satisfaction questionnaires. According to Weech-Maldonado et
al,12 to cross-culturally assess patient satisfaction, a questionnaire must be “conceptually
and technically equivalent to the source language, culturally competent, and linguistically
appropriate for the target population.” Specifically, a study showed that between the
English (n = 851) and Spanish (n = 113) CAHPS, at least some bias existed; however, the
bias did not meaningfully alter conclusions from the questionnaire, supporting the
Spanish translation as an effective tool.13 The CAHPS and other surveys have been
criticized for not addressing healthcare quality factors that are important to racial/ethnic
minorities but not Caucasian patients.14 Ignoring these factors may be, in part, why
some satisfaction questionnaires are deemed bias. If cross-cultural satisfaction
measurements are inaccurate and cultural competency expectations are not met,
patient satisfaction will be low or unknown; patients will seek care elsewhere, and
physicians will lose money.5 Additional research is necessary in this area to link cultural
competency, satisfaction, diversity, and health disparity.
Cultural competency education approaches are diverse and have been shown to
improve physician knowledge, skills, and attitudes. Three of the six Accreditation Council
for Graduate Medical Education core competencies involve cultural competency. The
core competencies of professionalism, interpersonal and communication skills, and
patient care require residents to demonstrate sensitivity and responsiveness to culture
in interactions with patients and colleagues7 (Resource 1). The widespread adoption;
consistency of program structure; and, ultimately, effectiveness of improving patient
healthcare outcomes must be investigated further to determine the true current state of
cultural competency training.15 Currently, cultural competence is left to organic
physician-patient interactions observed by medical trainees who readily mimic how to
act. Therefore, leadership plays a critical role in establishing norms and a culture of
understanding the value of diversity and cultural competency;1 however, more structure
is required to meet demands. According to one study, 96% of residents felt that the
inclusion of cultural competency education in training was important; however, almost
one-half of residents said that they received little to no instruction beyond medical
school.1,7 This may be the result of lack of time and role models because it is not viewed
as a priority among other training.1 Faculty may not have appropriate training in cultural
competence and patient communication necessary to formally teach these skills to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
8/25

residents.1 Through competency education, knowledge, awareness, attitudes, and skills
are developed, resulting in enhanced communication and improved patient
interactions.1,5 To fill the vacancy in training, the American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons (AAOS) created the AAOS Communication Skills Mentoring Program, which
trains mentors to facilitate workshops that act as a jumping off point for communication
with patients who speak limited English.1
This information seeks to educate physicians in a manner that benefits patients. Many
programs may simply highlight differences that divide individuals from different cultures.
Stereotyping or conflating culture with poverty or violence is easy but wrong.7 Additional
research and funding are necessary to develop programs that promote effective cultural
competency education.
Shared Decision Making
Shared decision making requires clear and effective communication, empathy, and the use of
decision aids.
Decision aids (video, print, web-based tools) enhance patient participation in decision making
and weighing advantages and risks of various treatment options.
Translators should be used with all limited English–speaking patients to improve patient
satisfaction and outcomes.
Professional in-person interpretation
A bilingual employee fluent in that language
Telephone services
Volunteers in some communities
Family, only if the patient offers or agrees; however, this is discouraged
Shared decision making is an “interpersonal, interdependent process in which the physician and
patient relate to and influence each other as they collaborate in making decisions.”3 Patient-
centered and culturally competent care result in good shared decision making.7 Legare et al16
identified three elements for shared decision making.6
Recognize and acknowledge that a decision is required.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
9/25

The patient and physician must know and understand the best available evidence concerning
the risks and advantages of each treatment option.
The decision must consider the provider’s guidance and the patient’s values and preferences.

Shared Decision Making
Barriers to shared decision making include time constraints, patient beliefs, the clinical
situation, and communicating uncertainty.6
Shared decision making requires clear empathetic communication. A presupposition
that the patient adequately comprehends health information exists. Variations in
opinions and expectations may be confusing, counterintuitive, and stressful for the
patient and treatment team. Poorly negotiated decision making may make obtaining
surgical consent, especially in the context of language or cultural conflicts, difficult.
Helping the patient fully understand risk, advantages, necessary treatment, and the level
of uncertainty is cruciate. Physicians may rely on enhanced support teams, using trained
health coaches, to aid in making a treatment decision. Patients with teams such as these
have 12.5% fewer hospital admissions and 9.9% fewer preference-sensitive surgeries.3
Decision aids are tools that may help patients participate in decisions that involve
weighing the advantages and risks of treatment options, often with scientific uncertainty.
Aids may take the form of print, video, or web-based tools. Decision aids have been
shown to optimize resource use without detracting from the patient experience. In
addition, decision aids improve knowledge, reduce decisional conflict, stimulate patients
to take a more active role in decision making, allow patients to choose less invasive or
less costly surgical treatment, and improve accurate risk perceptions.3 A randomized
trial of 123 patients with hip or knee osteoarthritis demonstrated that a video and
booklet in combination with a trained health coach telephone call improved informed
decision making and patient confidence in asking their physician questions.17 In
addition, patients with more substantial hip or knee osteoarthritis were more inclined to
pursue surgical treatment, whereas the marginal candidates, who had less to gain from
surgical treatment elected to undergo nonsurgical approaches.18 Shared decision
making has yet to be implemented widely in orthopaedic practices. Limited adoption
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
10/25

may include time and resource constraints or the fee-for-service payment system.3
Financial incentives and designating decision aids as quality measures may accelerate
adoption. Special consideration should be given to making aids available in multiple
languages.
The use of interpreters should be incorporated into patient communication. Despite
improving patient satisfaction, interpreters are underused by physicians.3 This may
relate to a greater time requirement per visit and more visits if an interpreter is required;
however, without interpreter services, decision making may be more cautious and
expensive.2 A physician receiving Medicaid or state-run children’s health insurance is
required by law to provide competent translation services if requested by patients who
speak limited English. Translation services may include the following:
A physician is legally obligated to see limited English–speaking patients on request and
cannot discharge them from a practice based on language. Interpreters should gain
status as a quality measure.
Bias
Physicians and patients may have implicit and explicit bias, which may affect quality of care
and patient satisfaction.

Bias
All individuals, to some extent, are consciously or unconsciously biased toward members
of a group different from themselves.5 Bias may be explicit or implicit. Explicit bias is
consciously choosing to not provide the same care based on a patient’s group identity.
Implicit bias is unconscious changes in behaviors because of observed group identity
resulting in disparate care. Physicians project their individual culture and values during
patient interactions. In a study of 248 trauma surgeons, 79% and 55% of respondents
claimed to favor no race or social class preferences, respectively; 74% of the trauma
surgeons demonstrated unconscious preference for White patients, and 91% of the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
11/25

trauma surgeons demonstrated unconscious preference for upper class patients.19
Being aware of one’s own culture, belief systems, values and knowledge, and biases and
how they interact with patients is important. Unconscious biases may affect clinical
decision making and contribute to healthcare disparities. Physicians with a negative
initial perception of an African American patient will affect compliance, satisfaction, and
outcome of treatment.5 It Physicians must explore their own beliefs, biases, and blind
spots. Resource 2 includes a link to the Implicit Associate Test.
Specific Ethnicities
According to the US census bureau, of the 328 million people living in the United States in
2019, 13.4% were African American (43.9 million), 18.5% were Hispanic (60.7 million), and 5.9%
were Asian American (1.94 million).
“You may have to treat people differently in order to treat them equally.”7
These observations of racial groups are not meant to stereotype or treat races as a monolith.
Rather, they are an attempt to clarify the sociocultural contexts in which patients live.
African American Patients
African American patients receive poorer quality health care, have higher morbidity and
mortality rates, and are less likely to perceive the benefits of widely accepted orthopaedic
treatments.
African American individuals may have considerable distrust of health care, especially medical
research.
Communication: May use different words for medical terminology (eg, sugar for diabetes
mellitus or miseries for pain); the patient should explain in his or her own words.5
Nontraditional medicine: may use a poultice (cataplasm), a soft moist mass, often heated and
medicated, that is spread on a cloth and placed over the skin to manage an aching, inflamed,
or painful part of the body; teas and concoctions also are common and may delay time to
treatment.5
Family: Ask about family dynamics directly. Patients have a strong sense of community,
family, friends, and neighborhood; multiple generations under one roof is not uncommon.5
Religion: Acknowledging and demonstrating respect for a patient’s religion may increase
adherence to treatment and may result in earlier consent of elderly patients to undergo
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
12/25

surgical treatment. Church members and a reverend may play a role in a patient’s medical
care. Twenty-two percent of individuals who are Jehovah Witnesses are African Americans (no
blood products).5

African American Patients
African American race was shown to be an independent variable of reported disparities.
Many may be wary of the White-dominated medical sector.5,7 Studies have reported that
African American patients face higher morbidity and mortality rates, experience higher
rates of major disease, wait longer for diagnosis, have more difficulty obtaining referrals
to subspecialists, and are more likely to recognize barriers to treatment.5 Specifically, for
orthopaedics, African Americans are less likely to receive adequate physical and
occupational therapy after a hip fracture or to undergo orthopaedic procedures, such as
joint arthroplasty.
African Americans’ view of health care is unique. Some believe that disease results from
natural causes, exposure to elements, or the will of God for improper behavior.5 Many
hold considerable distrust of medical care and research because of experience, friends,
relatives, or history of societal abuse.5 In such circumstances, surgeons should describe
safeguards to prevent abuse, a talk that may require multiple discussions to address
evolving concerns.5
Hispanic/Latino Patients
Largest ethnic minority population
Spanish speakers are more likely to have higher mortality, especially if uninsured.
Nontraditional medicine: may visit a sobador seeking massage therapy for musculoskeletal
pain (sprains, strains);5 botanicas are freestanding stores that diagnose diseases and sell
herbal medication.5
Family: Family is a strong unit with the father at the head.5 Adult Latino men may exhibit a
machismo attitude, or overly assertive masculine behavior, to decline medical care.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
13/25

Religion: New immigrants may believe the future is preordained and, therefore, decline
medical care. This belief is known as fatalism.5

Hispanic/Latino Patients
By 2040, 25% of the US population will be Hispanic/Latino.5,7 Asking an immigrant the
country from which they have emigrated from is appropriate because Hispanic/Latino
patients come from many countries, including Mexico, Cuba, South and Central America,
Puerto Rico, and Europe. Many respect physicians; therefore, physicians should act
formal.5,7 Hispanic/Latino patients have a higher mortality rate and are more likely to
sustain penetrating trauma. Approximately 10.4% of Hispanic/Latino individuals are
uninsured, which increases mortality.
Asian American Patients
5% of the US population is Asian; Asian Americans are more formal and group oriented
compared with Americans.
Many Asian cultures incorporate traditional medical philosophies and herbal therapies.
Nontraditional medicine: Specifically inquire about alternative medicine, such as herbal
supplements, or beliefs in holistic medicine. The patient may not admit to these practices
because of the perception that American doctors discourage self-medication. In addition,
Asian American patients, especially older patients, may not trust invasive modern medical
treatment or surgical treatment.5 Many herbal supplements alter hematologic parameters
and coagulation and, therefore, are a problem for surgical treatment. Ask about ingestion of
guilinggao, feverfew, qingkailing, danshen, ginseng, gingko biloba, and ginger.

Asian American Patients
Seventy percent of Asian individuals in the United States are immigrants, 90% of whom
are Chinese, Filipino, Indian, Vietnamese, Korean, or Japanese.5,7 Asian Americans tend
to have higher rates of education: 28% of Americans have a bachelor’s degree compared
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
14/25

with 50% of Indians and 27% of Vietnamese.5 In a registry for total knee replacement,
Asian American patients had twice the risk of premature coronary artery disease and
metabolic syndrome compared with Caucasian patients. According to a study, Asian
American patients had higher rates of implant failure and deep vein thrombosis after
knee arthroplasty.5 Further complicating this disparity, 16.8% of Asian Americans are
uninsured.
Asian Americans tend to be group oriented, considerate, modest, hierarchical, and
formal.5,7 Asian culture is quite different from White American culture in many respects.
“If a White American doctor is caring for an Asian-American patient, there is potential for
misunderstanding based on each person’s perception of the other. The physician may
interpret quietness as lack of assertion, modesty as inability to stand out, formality as
being ill at ease, lack of questioning as being noninquisitive, and respect for the doctor
as lack of independent thinking.”5
Because of their group-oriented nature, a cultural tendency to pool resources and care
for elderly family members in their own home exists. Surgeons must be very respectful
with older patients and realize that some patients will not accept becoming a financial
burden despite requiring medical care.5 Patients also may disagree with a treatment
strategy but not speak their mind, which is known as saving face.5 Open and honest
dialogue playing into the patient’s culture and preferences to improve adherence and
understanding is important.
Racial and Sex Diversity in Orthopaedics
Overview
Orthopaedic surgery has the lowest representation of females and minorities of all medical
and surgical subspecialties: African American, 1.5%; Hispanic/Latino, 1.7%; Asian American,
6.7%; female, 6.5%.1,7,20
Healthcare team diversity promotes additional diversity, innovation, cultural competency, and
patient satisfaction.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
15/25


Overview
The racial and sex composition of the orthopaedic community do not reflect the
populations they treat, leading to healthcare disparities for minorities. The AAOS has
made diversity a goal, even creating the Diversity Advisory Board. Diversity refers to the
differences that exist between individuals typically associated with race, sex, or culture.
Newer definitions have expanded the meaning to include other factors, such as
perspectives, social roles, and experiences.20 No standard exists for evaluating
representation in medicine; however, many studies use percentage of a group.21 Recent
studies, adjust for the demographic population in the United States, which reflects a
more accurate representation of inclusion.
Many benefits are associated with a diverse physician population. Underrepresented
minority (URM) physicians are more likely to have cultural competency with minority
patients, if for no other reason than life experiences.10 Diversity reduces healthcare
disparities and improves communication, patient care, and innovation.10 Black and
Hispanic physicians are more likely to care for underserved populations, including racial
minorities, Medicaid recipients, and uninsured patients.1,10,21,22 Diverse faculty
improves the ability of institutions to train physicians and medical students to practice in
racially diverse populations.10,21 URM physicians also promote and conduct biomedical
research that addresses disparities in healthcare access and outcomes in marginalized
communities, with improved recruitment for research in general.1,21 Patients should be
given the option to see race-concordant physicians, which promotes patient satisfaction,
patient participation in decision making, a sense of empathy, and better
outcomes.1,5,10,21,23 Patients notice if a healthcare team is more diverse and may be
more comfortable believing that the team or hospital respects cultural competency and
diversity.
Residents and Fellows
In 2019, 14% of orthopaedic residents were female. In 2016, 4% of orthopaedic surgery
residents were African American, 5.4% were Hispanic/Latino, and 0.2% were Native American.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001157
16/25

Female orthopaedic surgeons are slowly gaining ground, whereas URM orthopaedic surgeons
seem to be declining.

Residents and Fellows
The field of orthopaedics has had the slowest increase in female residents of any
specialty.20 Accompanying this trend, from 2005 to 2014, on average, White, Asian
American, African American, and Hispanic/Latino individuals matched into orthopaedics
at 73%, 68.5%, 46.4%, and 47.6%, respectively.24 This trend may be explained by the
leaky pipeline theory, which postulates that “the sequential loss of URM and females
interested in orthopaedic surgery throughout the educational pipeline from high school
to residency contributes to the lack of diversity in residency programs.”24 Recent studies
have demonstrated that some barriers to orthopaedic surgery occur at the residency
level because URM and female residents proportionally vary with medical student
representation. Other factors may include URM applicants applying to orthopaedic
surgery at lower rates compared with White and Asian American applicants. The location
of the medical school or being an orthopaedic surgery–inclined medical school did not
substantially affect application rate.6,12 Emphasis on United States Medical Licensing
Examination test scores and Alpha Omega Alpha membership also contribute to fewer
URM applicants.24 Experiences that exemplify interpersonal intelligence; overcoming
obstacles; and noncognitive factors, such as perseverance, conscientiousness, and grit,
which seem to correlate with success in residency selection and training better than
examination scores, transcripts, or structured interviews is important to consider1,25,26
(Video 1).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:48 AM
AAOS | Cultural Competence

Orthopaedic fellowships have not become more racially or sex diverse in the past
decade.22 Residency graduation rate declined from 59.2% to 46.1% for African American
students and from 59.0% to 26.3% for Hispanic/Latino students if adjusted for
population from 2005 to 2014.10,26 Women have seen a substantial increase only in
proportion; however, this was secondary to increased female residents. Even with
blinding reviewers to fellowship programs, no substantial difference was found between
the proportion of females versus males in blinded and unblinded groups. Currently,
White individuals disproportionately represent sports medicine, hand surgery, and
trauma; Asian individuals disproportionately represent reconstructive and spine surgery;
and women disproportionately represent pediatrics, oncology, and hand surgery.
Additional research is necessary to determine barriers and incentives for selecting or
avoiding specialties and fellowships.
Many solutions have been proposed to improve orthopaedic resident diversity, including
early interest interventions, pipeline programs, mentoring, deliberate selection, diversity
goals, and requiring cultural proficiency.10,27,28 The breadth of solutions speak to a

Attendings
The composition of current orthopaedic surgeons is Caucasian (90%), African American
(1.5%), Hispanic (1.7%), Asian American (6.7%), and female (6.5%).1,10 Current trends
project that female representation is trending slightly upward; however, women are
underrepresented in orthopaedic surgery at the associate level, at the full professor
level, and in department chair positions.20,21 URM orthopaedic surgeons are trending
toward greater underrepresentation, being underrepresented at the assistant, associate,
and full professor levels from 1990 to 2016. These disparity in representation may be
driven by biases in hiring, promotion, and compensation that may limit female or URM
faculty. Current strategies to increase representation are inadequate to meet the needs
of a rapidly diversifying patient population. More aggressive measures for recruitment,
retention, and promotion are necessary.21 One solution may involve using the Rooney
Rule, a policy created by the National Football League, which requires at least one URM
to be interviewed for a head coaching position.1,10,23 A policy such as this may be the
first step in improving diversity in orthopaedics at the faculty level, which, would ease
the difficulty of URM and female recruitment.20
Initiatives to Improve Diversity
The field of orthopaedic surgery can be diversified via a commitment to actively recruit,
pipeline programs, early exposure, and mentoring.

Pipeline programs, such as Nth Dimension and the Perry Initiative, have been shown to be
successful in improving female and URM orthopaedic application rates, acceptance, and
retention.
The field of orthopaedic surgery is unlikely to drastically improve female and URM
representation in the short-term;1 therefore, the field should invest in teaching cultural
competency and make long-term investments in enhanced recruitment strategies and
research.
Nth Dimension (founded in 2006) targets junior female and URM medical students in
orthopaedic surgery via hands-on surgical simulation and skills workshops. The program
demonstrated odds ratios of 43.2 for women (P < .001) and 14.5 for URMs (P < .001) for
applying to orthopaedic surgery residency. Seventy-six percent of applicants who went
through the program successfully matched into orthopaedic surgery.10,20 In a study, 100% of
students who completed the Nth Dimension remain in or have completed their orthopaedic
residency.28
The Perry Initiative (founded in 2009) targets high school girls to improve perceptions of and
overall interest in orthopaedic surgery.
The J. Robert Gladden Orthopaedic Society (founded in 1998) provides URM medical students
with mentorship, mock oral examinations, traveling fellowship programs, and grants.
The Ruth Jackson Orthopaedic Society (founded in 1983) is devoted to advancing women in
orthopaedic surgery. It provides opportunities such as mentorship, scholarships, research
grants and awards, educational projects, an endowment with the Orthopaedic Research and
Education Foundation, and a traveling fellowship program.

Initiatives to Improve Diversity
Diversity is a reciprocal issue. If patients, applicants, medical students, residents, or
attendings are made to feel like outliers, they may be more difficult to recruit.10 Medical
schools with more URM orthopaedic residents and faculty had substantially increased
URM applicants.11 More programs with diverse residents who feel comfortable are
required before any major changes in representation can occur. Active recruitment of
diverse applicants should be considered. In most cases, diversity will not simply happen;
rather, institutions that are diverse are diverse by design.27 Initiatives have been

Improving an early interest in orthopaedic surgery can be fostered via workshops,
events, and mentoring. Early exposure to musculoskeletal didactic courses has been
shown to improve interest in orthopaedics, with minority students particularly

In such instances, faculty must demonstrate, via mentorship, that a successful career
